bull_thesis:
BULL THESIS — FICO (Fair Isaac), price $1,239.91, base conviction B/4, signal = catalyst (mortgage-score repricing).

CORE CLAIM: FICO is a regulated, embedded monopoly that has discovered it was dramatically under-pricing its single most mission-critical product, and is now harvesting that mispricing on a multi-year ramp. The financials corroborate that this is a real, durable step-change in unit economics — not financial engineering — and the market's ~27% drawdown from ~$1,700 (2026-Q1) to ~$1,251 (2026-Q2) has handed the position a margin of safety the screener pegs at 56% (Price 1239.91 vs Fair Value 1935.89).

(1) THE ENGINE IS REAL AND THE NUMBERS CONFIRM IT, NOT JUST THE FRAMING. Across the multi-year trajectory the durable compounding is undeniable: revenue 1.32B (2021) -> 1.99B (2025); net income 392M -> 652M; EPS 13.4 -> 26.54, a 5-yr EPS CAGR of +18.6% with the most recent year at +29.8% YoY. The dossier's own forensic table verdicts are overwhelmingly corroborative: revenue growth "Lumpy but real," margin expansion "Corroborated... genuinely elite SaaS-like margins," EPS "Strong," FCF "Corroborated. Cash conversion is excellent" (FCF +26.7% YoY, FCF margin 38.7%, "$867M over last 4 quarters, +28%," 2026-Q2). Gross margin is 82.2% and expanding, net margin 32.7%. ROIC is 41.0% — the dossier explicitly flags that "capital is productively deployed despite negative book equity." This is the unit-economics profile of a toll-road, not a cyclical.

(2) THE PRICING POWER IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PROMOTIONAL — THE MOAT IS REGULATORY EMBEDMENT. The bull case rests on the dossier's green flag that pricing power "is structural — FICO is embedded across underwriting, securitization, rating, and capital adequacy ('used in many, many places downstream,' 2025-Q4); the per-closed-loan model monetizes previously un-captured IP." FICO's score is wired into the entire mortgage value chain (origination, GSE eligibility, securitization, ratings, capital adequacy), so the cost to rip it out vastly exceeds the price. Management's repeated, disciplined pre-justification — "FICO's share is only about two-tenths of 1%... the lowest of all individual mortgage closing costs" (2024-Q4) — is not spin; it quantifies exactly how much headroom remains. A product that is ~0.2% of closing cost and indispensable has years of pricing runway. The $4.95 royalty -> Direct License Program -> performance-pricing ($0.99/score + funding fee) is a staged monetization of an asset that was mispriced for a decade.

(3) THE CATALYST IS LIVE AND ACCELERATING. Mortgage originations ran +127% YoY and reached 63% of total Scores revenue (2026-Q2), up from 37% (2024-Q4). The tone trajectory is "RISING," culminating in "very strong quarter... increasing our fiscal 2026 guidance" (2026-Q2) and "deal size is going up, the frequency... and the amounts" (2026-Q1). Critically, the price increases are already locked: management is "deliberately vague on volume... but precise on price ('the price is extremely well understood... here for the year,' 2026-Q1)." That means a large fraction of the 2026 uplift is contractually de-risked regardless of where rates go — the bull does not need a mortgage volume boom, only that volume not collapse, because per-loan price is already reset upward.

(4) GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY IS HIGH AND DATA-VALIDATED — THE COMPANY UNDER-PROMISES. The dossier scores guidance credibility "HIGH," corroborated by an 86% beat rate (6/7 quarters). The sandbagging is openly admitted methodology: "we build a model... then we will take that and haircut that expectation... we don't want to be sweating out the fourth quarter" (2025-Q4). When Craig Huber baited them — "well positioned to well exceed guidance" — Weber confirmed "you'd probably still think we were being too conservative" (2026-Q1). They reiterated FY26 guidance in Q1 then raised in Q2 after "a better second quarter volume-wise than we had anticipated." A management team with a documented, financials-validated habit of beating is exactly who you want owning a multi-year price ramp: reported numbers are more likely to surprise up than down.

(5) MANAGEMENT IS BUYING THEIR OWN PULLBACK, AND SO ARE INSIDERS. Insider buy ratio is 1.05 (net buying). The company repurchased $605M in 2026-Q2 at ~$1,251 and management explicitly called it "an opportunistic time" — "I would certainly consider our stock at these levels to be an opportunistic time" (2026-Q2). When the people with the most information are net buyers at the same ~$1,240 level the committee is being asked to buy, that is a strong corroborating signal. The dossier notes the capital-allocation tone shifted "from philosophical ('screaming value,' 2024-Q4) to tactically opportunistic" — they are signaling the post-pullback price is attractive to them.

(6) THE OPTIONALITY IS FREE: SOFTWARE/AI IS A CALL OPTION YOU AREN'T PAYING FOR. The market is valuing FICO on Scores; Software is treated as anemic (seg +2% to +7% revenue). But the leading indicators are inflecting: ACV TTM +36%, "$126M" (2026-Q2), platform ARR "$254M (2025-Q3) then... approaching $350M (2026-Q2)," platform net retention 124%, "FY26 ACV bookings significantly higher than FY25" (2026-Q1), Gartner DI leader, and a new sales leader (Nikhil Behl promoted to EVP Software, 2024-Q3) that "correlates with subsequent bookings acceleration." The AI re-skinning ("agentic-by-design," "FICO FFM foundation model," 137 AI patents -> 230+ issued patents) plus Lansing's explainability moat point — "AI is limited by strict regulatory requirements on explainability" (2026-Q2) — is precisely the defense that protects scoring from LLM commoditization. If software revenue ever catches its bookings, that is upside the current multiple ignores.

(7) VALUATION IS DEMANDING BUT DEFENSIBLE FOR THIS QUALITY. P/FCF ~39.6x for a business compounding FCF mid-teens-to-high-20s with 82% gross / 38.7% FCF margins, 41% ROIC, a quasi-regulatory monopoly, structural pricing power, and validated sandbagging is a premium — but the screener's DCF still implies a 56% margin of safety to a $1,935.89 fair value. The recent 27% derating from ~$1,700 to ~$1,251 means much of the multiple compression risk has already been taken; you are entering after the air came out, with insiders and the company buying alongside you.

KEY CONDITIONS THE BULL CASE REQUIRES (each must hold):
- Mortgage volume does not suffer a sustained air-pocket. Because price is locked but "your guess is as good as ours" on rates (repeated), a multi-quarter origination collapse could overwhelm the per-loan price gains. The bull needs volume merely stable-to-modestly-down, not booming.
- The per-score vs. performance-fee split (which management admits "we frankly don't know," 2025-Q4) lands neutral-to-favorable. This is "the biggest unmodeled revenue swing factor."
- FHFA/GSE/VantageScore regulatory outcomes do not force a structural re-rating of FICO's mandated position. The bull leans on management's framing that even GSE privatization helps ("credit-default risk emphasis goes up = advantage FICO," 2026-Q2) and that there is "no share loss... in any vertical" with mid-90s share.
- Margins hold near current levels even though they sit "1.38 sigma above historical peak"; some mean reversion is tolerable, a collapse is not.

If those hold, you own a regulated monopoly mid-cycle through a multi-year repricing of its crown-jewel product, run by a credible, net-buying management team, at a 56% discount to intrinsic value after a 27% pullback. That is an asymmetric, high-quality compounder entry.
bear_thesis:
BEAR THESIS — FICO (Fair Isaac), price $1,239.91, base conviction B/4.

CORE CLAIM: The recent EPS acceleration the bull is paying ~40x FCF for is a one-time repricing of a single monopoly product into the most rate-sensitive, regulation-exposed end market in finance — and the company is now MORE concentrated, MORE levered, and MORE statistically stretched than at any point in its history, precisely when the multiple is being asked to stay premium. The "39%/60-69%" growth narrative management leads with materially overstates a durable trajectory that is roughly HALF that. You are anchoring to the windfall, not the run-rate.

(1) THE HEADLINE GROWTH IS LARGELY A ONE-TIME REPRICING, AND THE DOSSIER SAYS SO EXPLICITLY. The single most important bear fact, in the dossier's own words: "the headline percentages management leads with (39%, 60-69%) materially overstate the durable trajectory (~16% revenue, ~23-30% EPS)... The richness vs. the numbers is in the framing of mortgage pricing as recurring growth when it is largely a one-time repricing of an existing monopoly." The screener confirms it: revenue +15.9% YoY (not 39%), 3-yr CAGR +13.1%; EPS +29.8% (not 60-69%). Management's revenue claim "up 39%" (2026-Q2) is verdicted "Lumpy but real... The 39% Q2 figure is heavily mortgage-price-driven, not a steady-state rate. The narrative cherry-picks the best quarter." When the price reset laps, growth reverts toward mid-teens, and a ~40x P/FCF multiple set against a +29.8% headline gets repriced against a +16% reality. That gap IS the bear case.

(2) EXTREME, RISING SINGLE-PRODUCT CONCENTRATION INTO A RATE-CYCLICAL END MARKET. Mortgage is now 63% of total Scores revenue (2026-Q2), up from 37% (2024-Q4) — the dossier's #1 red flag: "The entire EPS acceleration rests on repricing one monopoly product into a rate-sensitive, regulation-exposed end market." Mortgage originations of +127% YoY are not a new normal; they are a volume spike layered on top of a price spike. Management is candidly blind on the volume half: "your guess is as good as ours" on rates (repeated). The bull's claim that "price is locked" does not save the thesis — a per-loan price that is 2x higher applied to a mortgage market that contracts 30-40% in a rate shock still produces a revenue and EPS air-pocket, and the comps would then be brutal because you are lapping BOTH a price reset AND a volume peak. This is the textbook setup for a violent de-rate: a cyclical peak masquerading as secular growth.

(3) NEGATIVE EQUITY AND DEBT-FUNDED BUYBACKS AT THE WRONG PRICE. ROE is -110.6% — the dossier is explicit this is "negative equity from buybacks," net debt $2.80B. The company "bought $605M in 2026-Q2 at $1,251 after buying back at $1,707 in 2026-Q1" — verdict: "Aggressive — flag... poor timing on the higher tranche." A balance sheet with negative book equity has no shock absorber: if the mortgage air-pocket hits while net debt sits at $2.80B and the equity cushion is gone, the financial flexibility to keep supporting the stock evaporates exactly when it is most needed. The bull reframes buybacks as an insider "buy signal"; the bear reads $1,707-then-$1,251 as management mis-timing its own capital while levering the balance sheet to do it. The insider buy ratio of 1.05 is barely above neutral — thin support for a "they're backing up the truck" narrative.

(4) MARGINS ARE STATISTICALLY STRETCHED — MEAN REVERSION IS A WHEN, NOT AN IF. The dossier flags margins at "1.38 sigma above historical peak — statistically stretched; mean-reversion risk if volume or pricing normalizes," and separately "near record, a caution on mean reversion." Gross 82.2%, FCF margin 38.7% are being extrapolated by the bull as durable; they are being earned at the top of the cycle on peak mortgage mix. If volume normalizes, mix shifts, or the performance-pricing split lands unfavorably, both the revenue line AND the margin compress simultaneously — a double hit to FCF that a 40x multiple cannot absorb.

(5) THE HIGHEST-GROWTH LINE IS UNMODELABLE — BY MANAGEMENT'S OWN ADMISSION. The performance-pricing model split ($0.99/score vs. performance/funding fee) is "the biggest unmodeled revenue swing factor and management cannot/will not quantify it" — "we frankly don't know what the split is going to be" (2025-Q4). You are being asked to pay a premium multiple for a revenue stream whose composition the company itself cannot forecast. Opacity at the exact point of maximum growth is a red flag, not a footnote. Add the recurring non-disclosures — declining to size credit-card originations revenue (2026-Q1), CCS usage headwinds deflected with "your guess is as good as ours" (2025-Q2) — and visibility into the consumption-driven and performance-fee lines is genuinely poor.

(6) THE "NO SHARE LOSS" MOAT IS ALREADY CRACKING ON THE RECORD. The bull leans on "no share loss... in any vertical." But the dossier captures management itself conceding the opposite under analyst pressure: on dual-score gaming (Sean Kennedy, 2026-Q2), Lansing admitted it is "almost inevitable... structural that one score or the other is going to be more beneficial" and that it is "technically share loss for FICO" — the dossier calls this "the clearest crack in the 'no share loss' claim." Meanwhile management is "genuinely blind" on the FHFA LLPA grid: "No idea. I have heard nothing... I encourage you guys to keep asking" (2026-Q2). VantageScore competition + FHFA's GSE-scoring decisions are live, adverse-tail regulatory events on the SAME product that is now 63% of Scores revenue. A single unfavorable FHFA/GSE ruling (mandating VantageScore acceptance, capping the royalty, or altering the LLPA grid) could permanently impair the crown jewel — and management has explicitly admitted it has zero visibility into the outcome.

(7) THE DEFENSIVE TELLS SUGGEST MANAGEMENT KNOWS WHERE THE BODIES ARE. The tone trajectory shows a clear "offensive->defensive shift": pricing is pre-justified on "every call since 2024-Q4," and regulatory answers are "rehearsed" — the "if GSEs go private... advantage FICO" framing is, per the dossier, "designed to convert every regulatory scenario into a bull case — a tell that they know this is the central investor anxiety." The reassurance "no surprises ahead... I don't see being blindsided" (2026-Q2) is itself flagged as "a tell when an analyst keeps asking." The AI moat-defense ("AI is limited by strict regulatory requirements on explainability") and the patent escalation (137 -> 230+) read as "reputational armor... pre-empting the bear case that LLMs disrupt scoring." Companies that rehearse the rebuttal to a thesis usually do so because the thesis has teeth.

(8) SOFTWARE IS NOT THE BAILOUT THE BULL WANTS IT TO BE. The bull's "free call option" is, on the reported numbers, a stalled engine: Software revenue grew only "2-7% across these quarters while Scores exploded," and the dossier verdict is "Mixed... the story is richer than the numbers justify." Bookings (ACV +36%) have been "significantly higher" for two years without converting to revenue — at some point unconverted bookings become a credibility problem, not a catalyst. If Scores decelerates and Software has still not inflected the revenue line, there is no second engine to cushion the de-rate.

WHAT WOULD CONFIRM THE BEAR:
- A sequential decline in mortgage origination volume (rate-driven) that drops Scores revenue despite locked pricing — the air-pocket. Watch the first quarter where +127% YoY comps roll over.
- The performance-pricing split landing unfavorably (more low-fee per-score, less funding fee), compressing the highest-growth line management can't forecast.
- Any FHFA/GSE/VantageScore action that mandates competitor acceptance, caps the royalty, or changes the LLPA grid — converting "technically share loss" into actual, structural share loss on the 63%-concentrated product.
- Margin reversion off the 1.38 sigma peak, hitting FCF as revenue growth simultaneously decelerates toward the ~16% durable rate.
- A further leg down in the stock forcing a buyback pause amid $2.80B net debt and negative equity, removing the technical bid.

BOTTOM LINE: You are paying ~40x FCF (premium) for a +16% durable revenue business dressed up as a +39% grower, with 63% of Scores revenue concentrated in a rate-cyclical, regulation-exposed product at a volume-and-price double peak, financed off a negative-equity balance sheet, with the fastest-growing revenue line admitted to be unforecastable and the "no share loss" moat already conceding "technically share loss." The 56% "margin of safety" is an artifact of a DCF extrapolating peak-cycle margins and growth. The asymmetry the bull sees inverts if mortgage volume rolls or FHFA rules wrong — and management's rehearsed defensiveness suggests they know it.

RESOLUTION-DRIVER INDEPENDENCE (regime rule d) — THE DECISIVE DEMERIT. The regime tells me to be wary of a thesis whose payoff hinges on the SAME shared macro factor as the broad market. FICO's entire near-term payoff hinges on mortgage ORIGINATION VOLUME, which is a direct function of the rate/inflation path that IS the central axis of this regime. The one bull-supportive positioning fact is the company's own buyback ($605M/quarter) as a standing bid plus management's stated willingness to be 'opportunistic' on weakness. ## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these eight quarters the FICO story underwent a regime change — not in the *business*, which performed flawlessly throughout, but in the *external structure* that surrounds the crown-jewel asset (the FICO Score's conforming-mortgage monopoly).

**Phase 1 (mid-2024 → early-2025): "Pricing-cycle compounder, monopoly intact, FHFA tailwind pending."** The early calls are a victory lap built on two engines: (a) the **mortgage Scores pricing cycle** — wholesale royalty raised to $4.95/score for CY2025 (Q4-FY24, 2024-11-06), with mortgage-origination revenue up *80% (Q3-FY24), 95% (Q4-FY24), 110% (Q1-FY25)* almost entirely on price; and (b) the **FICO Score 10-T conforming-adoption catalyst** — the pending FHFA mandate to replace Classic FICO with 10-T for GSE loans. **The first crack (2025-02-04, Q1-FY25):** Lansing disclosed, almost in passing, that *"In January, the FHFA announced it no longer has a specific timeline for the implementation"* of 10-T for conforming mortgages. **Classification: STABLE business / PIVOTING competitive structure.** The operating company is strengthening (accelerating revenue, record FCF, expanding margins, disciplined buybacks). But the *investment case* is pivoting from "unassailable sole-source monopoly compounding at a premium multiple" to "dominant-but-now-contested data franchise re-rating to a competitive multiple while harvesting one final, enormous price/volume cycle." This is a *deep-value re-rate-the-multiple* thesis, **not** an asymmetric special-situation catalyst. Size it as a quality-compounder-on-sale, not as an event trade — and respect that the one hard data point on conviction (insider open-market activity) is *zero buys, four sells.*

bull_thesis:
Fair Isaac still owns the most predictive credit score in American mortgage lending, and that is now documented by someone other than Fair Isaac. Using the loan-level performance data Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac released on 1 July 2026, the actuarial firm Milliman found FICO Score 10T beats VantageScore 4.0 on all three standard measures of predictive power, in every origination year tested, with more than a 10% advantage on first-time buyers and more than 8% on the newest loans. Both models are built on the same underlying credit files, so the gap is modelling skill, not data access. That is the asset.

The business built on it is performing. In the June 2026 quarter revenue reached $674 million, up 26% on the year; reported earnings were $10.45 a share, up 41%; adjusted operating margin expanded 479 basis points to 62%; and trailing free cash flow reached $961 million, up 28%, on capital spending of roughly 0.2% of revenue. Management raised full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to $2.53 billion of revenue, up 20%, with adjusted earnings of $42.43 a share, up 42%. At $928.30 that is about 22 times this year's adjusted earnings for a company earning a 59% return on invested capital.

The bull case has three legs. First, the competition may take far less than the market now fears. The chief executive's argument on the July 2026 call is that a two-score market creates score shopping, and score shopping requires pulling both scores to know which one flatters the borrower. On that logic FICO keeps the pull even where the rival score gets submitted, which is why the company reported no volume loss at all through June while the rival was already near 20% share at the largest originators. Lansing puts the rival's theoretical ceiling in the 20s for exactly this reason.

Second, the software business has quietly become a real asset. Platform annual recurring revenue reached $413 million in the June quarter, up 62%, and crossed above the legacy book for the first time in company history. Platform revenue retention is 148%, trailing bookings are $128 million and up 39%, and excluding migrations platform revenue still grew in the high 30s. The headline segment growth of 2% badly understates this, because it nets a fast-growing new business against a legacy book management is deliberately retiring. A next-generation platform with an enterprise fraud product reaches general availability later this calendar year, and an Accenture distribution partnership signed in July 2026 addresses the sales-reach problem directly.

Third, the company has not run out of ways to get paid. Score 10T becomes available to Federal Housing Administration lenders on 1 January 2027 on a fixed, binding date. 10T is bundled free with the classic score today, and Lansing said plainly in July 2026 that One could easily imagine a revenue jump at FICO if we were to charge separately for the two. The direct-licence programme, once the remaining government-sponsored enterprise certifies it, introduces a funding-fee model that charges per closed loan rather than per credit pull, which is structurally immune to score shopping. Agreements already cover resellers representing about 60% of mortgage volume with negotiations under way toward 90%. Beyond mortgage there is auto, card, personal loan, the new cash-flow UltraFICO score built with Plaid, and international.

For this to work, three things must hold: the calendar-2027 mortgage rate card must not be cut materially; lenders must keep pulling a FICO score even when they submit a rival one; and the platform business must keep compounding above 40% so that within three years the company is no longer a single-product story. If all three hold, the sum of the parts supports roughly $1,195 a share.
bear_thesis:
Roughly 42% of this company's revenue is one product, sold at one price, into one regulated channel, and on 4 September 2026 the regulator removed the barrier that protected it.

The arithmetic first. In the June 2026 quarter the Scores segment was $459 million of $674 million in total revenue, mortgage originations were 62% of Scores, and mortgage-origination revenue grew 97% on low-single-digit volume growth. Almost none of that growth is volume. It is the calendar-2026 rate card, which took the mortgage score from $4.95 to $10. In the March 2026 quarter the same line grew 127%. This is a price increase being reported as growth, and it carries close to 100% incremental margin, which is why the margin expansion looks so impressive and why it is so fragile.

That price is now indefensible in the open. On 4 September 2026 the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to accept VantageScore 4.0 from every approved originator, effective immediately, ending a four-month pilot that had been capped at 50 lenders; on 9 September the enterprises removed the prior-written-approval requirement entirely. The agency's director publicly criticised Fair Isaac's pricing, citing roughly an 1,800% increase in the per-score price since 2020, following an investigation opened by Senator Hawley in March. The shares fell about 21% in a single session on 4 September and are 53% below their 52-week high of $1,998.

The distribution structure makes this worse than a normal competitive threat. Fair Isaac does not sell scores to lenders; the three credit bureaus do. Those same bureaus own VantageScore. Equifax is selling VantageScore 4.0 at $4.50, more than 50% below the FICO price, through the end of 2027; TransUnion cut it to $0.99 and is bundling it free with a FICO purchase through 2026. Fair Isaac's distributors are its competitor's owners, and they are now pricing the substitute at a tenth of its price with the regulator's blessing.

Management's defence is that score shopping requires pulling both scores, so FICO keeps the pull. That defence depends on the rival score costing money. It does not. And management admitted on the same July 2026 call that it cannot independently verify the point: asked how easily it could detect volume loss, Lansing answered it is not that easy, honestly, it is not that easy. One quarter earlier, in April 2026, the company had told the market it did not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical. By July the rival was near 20% share at UWM and Rocket. A forward statement of that importance, reversed in 91 days, is a forecasting record the market should not extrapolate from.

The balance sheet has lost its shock absorber. In the June 2026 quarter, nine weeks before the regulatory decision, the company bought back 1.705 million shares for $1.96 billion at an average price of $1,149 and part-funded it with a new $1.5 billion term loan. Across fiscal 2026 it spent roughly $2.7 billion on its own stock at an average near $1,195, against $928.30 today: about $600 million of value destroyed in nine months. Total debt is $5.58 billion at a 5.64% weighted average rate, net debt roughly $5.35 billion, and net leverage 4.2 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, against 1.4 times at S&P Global, 1.5 at Moody's and 2.4 at Verisk. Forty per cent of that debt is floating-rate term loans and revolver, in the month the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time since 2023 with sixteen of eighteen policymakers pointing to another. Leverage turns an earnings problem into an equity problem.

The second business does not yet carry the company. Software grew 2% in the June quarter. The legacy book is shrinking 25% in revenue and 17% in recurring revenue with an 82% retention rate. The platform half is genuinely excellent but is still only $413 million of recurring revenue against a $20 billion market value.

Finally, the mortgage market itself offers no rescue. Lansing said in July 2026 that elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges continue to weigh on the mortgage market, keeping loan originations below historical norms. Since then the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007 and the thirty-year mortgage sits near 6.95%. Any thesis requiring a volume recovery is a rate-cut thesis, and rates are going the other way.

What confirms the bear: a calendar-2027 rate card published at a materially lower price, the first quarter in which FICO pull volume falls below mortgage application volume, or another quarter of the direct-licence certification failing to arrive. On a reduced price and a lost share of pulls, the parts are worth roughly $420 a share.

The cohort de-rated together on shared drivers - mortgage volume and federal credit-score policy - so that gap is sector movement, not an edge specific to this company. Second, the market regime works against the volume half of the bull case. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September 2026 with most policymakers pointing to another, the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007 and the thirty-year mortgage sits near 6.95%. Any part of the thesis requiring an origination recovery is a rate-cut thesis, and we discount those rather than pay for them.

On the catalyst: the event that mattered has already happened and the fall it caused is spent. In this book that is neither a mark for nor against - we judge the value left over, and the value left over is roughly the price. The same reasoning applies to the fixed 1 January 2027 date at the Federal Housing Administration: it is real and binding, but it admits the rival on the same day, so it is not an asymmetry in this company's favour.

# Forensic Dossier — Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO)

**Prepared 2026-09-22 · price used $928.30 (NYSE, US dollars) · transcripts covered: Q2 FY25 (2025-04-29) through Q3 FY26 (2026-07-29, pulled live because the archived file stops at 2026-04-28)**

Fair Isaac sells two things. The first is the FICO Score — the credit score that roughly nine in ten large American lenders use, and which until three weeks ago was effectively the only score Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac would accept on a mortgage. The second is FICO Platform, enterprise software that banks use to make lending and fraud decisions. The Score business is small in revenue and enormous in profit; the software business is the reverse. Almost everything that matters about this company right now concerns the first one.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**Spring 2025 — the price lever is working, quietly.** In the April 2025 call management led with 15% revenue growth and mortgage-origination revenue up 48% on a modest price increase. Score 10T, the newer model, was being given away free alongside the classic score to build adoption. The story was: a durable franchise, priced below its worth, gradually closing the gap.

**Summer 2025 — the regulator arrives.** By July 2025 the tone had shifted to defence. Lansing referenced "the recent FHFA announcement" and immediately pivoted to adoption statistics — $313 billion of annualised originations signed to the 10T adopter programme. The subtext: when the mandate goes, adoption will be our moat instead.

**Autumn 2025 — deliberate conservatism.** The November 2025 call is the most revealing on guidance philosophy. Weber: "we build a model that we believe is what's likely to happen. And then we will take that and haircut that expectation… it's probably a little bit more of a haircut that went into that because there's so much uncertainty." Lansing added that although "there's a good chance rates will come down, big volume increases associated with rate declines are not built into our guidance." This is a management team that has systematically under-promised — and, as Section 4 shows, has been rewarded for it.

**Winter–spring 2026 — the price shock lands, and so does the regulator's counter.** The calendar-2026 rate card took the mortgage score from $4.95 to $10. Second-quarter fiscal 2026 (April 2026) was the blow-off: revenue up 39%, Scores up 60%, **mortgage-origination revenue up 127% year over year** on low-single-digit volume growth. Almost all of that was price. In the same call management disclosed it had rewritten the pricing architecture for its direct-licence programme — from $4.95 per score plus a $33 funding fee to **$0.99 per score plus a $65 funding fee** — an explicit move from charging per credit pull to charging per closed loan. That is a defensive redesign dressed as an innovation, and it was announced the week after the housing regulator's credit-score modernisation update.

**Summer 2026 — the story contracts.** By July 2026 the growth rate had halved (Scores up 41%, mortgage revenue up 97%), and Lansing was conceding what he had denied one quarter earlier: VantageScore was running near 20% of conforming volume at the largest originators. His framing — that lenders "game" by pulling both scores, so FICO loses no volume — is the load-bearing assumption of the entire remaining bull case.

**The arc in one line:** a pricing story that compounded for four years has become a regulatory story, and management's narrative has moved from *how much more can we charge* to *how do we keep getting paid at all*.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Mortgage revenue +97% on **low-single-digit** volume | **Diverges sharply.** Company growth is one product line's price increase. Strip mortgage price and the business grows in the high single digits. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — and the decline is in the answers, not the prepared remarks.**

The scripted portions stay uniformly confident across all six calls. The change is in the question-and-answer sessions.

- *April 2025:* expansive and offensive. Kenya scores, financial-literacy campaigns, the mortgage simulator. Growth language throughout.
- *November 2025:* first defensive note, framed as prudence. "It's a lot easier to raise your guidance than it is to lower it."

A chief executive asking sell-side analysts to find out what his regulator is doing is a visibility problem stated out loud.

Asked what FICO would do about pricing in response, he declined: "there are many, many things that FICO can do and we're not in a position to share them on this call."

The vocabulary has shifted from *monetisation* and *innovation* to *gaming*, *degrees of freedom*, *theoretical maximum* and *we'll have to wait and see*. Guidance has become **more** specific on the numbers and **less** specific on the drivers — the classic pattern of a management team confident in the next two quarters and unwilling to describe the two after that.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability on delivery: High. Reliability on strategic forecasting: Low.**

The delivery record is close to unimpeachable. Fiscal 2025 guidance was exceeded "on all metrics." Fiscal 2026 guidance was reiterated in the first quarter, raised in the second and raised again in the third, ending at $2.53B of revenue (+20%), $36.86 of reported earnings per share (+39%) and $42.43 on the adjusted basis (+42%). The screener's 6-of-7 quarterly beat rate (86%) matches. Weber describes the sandbagging openly, which is itself a credibility marker — a team that tells you it haircuts its own model is not hiding the haircut.

The strategic forecasting record is the opposite. Three specific failures:

1. **Competitive share.** "We do not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical" (April 2026) survived one quarter.
2. **The direct-licence programme.** Promised as imminent since the first quarter of fiscal 2026 ("one large reseller is close to completing production integration testing"), it is still, in July 2026, "waiting on certification from one of the GSEs so that we can go live." Three consecutive quarters of *almost*. Management's defence — Lansing in January 2026, "whether it comes a little sooner or a little later, does not have a big revenue impact on us" — was then contradicted in July when Weber attributed part of the guidance *raise* to the programme **not** going live, because going live would have pushed revenue out.
3. **Detectability.** The company cannot independently verify its own volume share and says so.

The pattern: FICO is highly reliable about what it will earn in the next ninety days and unreliable about the structure of its market beyond that. For a name whose entire investment case is now structural rather than quarterly, that is the wrong half of the record to be good at.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts have been circling the same three questions for six quarters and have not been given an answer to any of them.

**Where does the price go next year?** Asked by Huber (January 2026) and Clinch (July 2026). Weber: "We don't disclose the specifics of it." Lansing, July 2026: "it's early days… No final decisions have been made about other — about any of the sectors, frankly, about mortgage or auto or card or personal." The calendar-2027 rate card is the single most valuable undisclosed number in the story and management will not be drawn on it.

**Are lenders actually dropping FICO pulls at submission?** Haas (Wells Fargo) and Sabadra (RBC) both asked directly in July 2026. Lansing's answer rests entirely on the gaming argument: you must pull both scores to know which flatters the borrower, therefore FICO's pull volume is protected. This holds only while both scores cost real money. TransUnion is bundling VantageScore 4.0 free with a FICO purchase through 2026, and Equifax is selling it at $4.50 against FICO's $10 through the end of 2027. The moment gaming becomes free, the argument that gaming protects FICO's volume inverts.

**What happens when the market has three scores?** Alwy (Deutsche Bank), July 2026. Lansing conceded the point: "that's kind of a shopping — a score shopping environment," and that retiring the classic score is "hard to imagine… not anytime soon." A franchise that must live inside a score-shopping market is not the franchise the multiple was built on.

**The question nobody asked:** not one analyst across six calls pressed management on the wisdom of spending $2.7B on its own stock at an average near $1,195, $1.96B of it borrowed, while the company's exclusivity was under active regulatory review. Kyle Peterson (Needham) came closest in July 2026 and framed it as a positive — "good to see the ASR big signal."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Concentration.** Mortgage-origination scores are 62% of Scores revenue and Scores is 68% of the company — roughly **42% of total revenue from one product in one regulated channel**, at near-100% incremental margin (Q3 FY26).

🔴 **The reversal.** "No share loss in any vertical" (Q2 FY26) → competitor at 20% share (Q3 FY26).

🔴 **Debt-funded buybacks into a regulatory cliff.** $1.96B at $1,149 average in the June 2026 quarter, funded with a $1.5B term loan, taking net leverage to 4.2x. The stock is 19% lower today.

🔴 **Floating-rate exposure into a tightening cycle.** 40% of $5.58B is term-loan and revolver debt, in a month when the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time since 2023.

🔴 **Non-platform software is shrinking fast.** Down 25% in revenue and 17% in annual recurring revenue in Q3 FY26, with an 82% retention rate. Management calls this deliberate end-of-life; some of it plainly is, but it means the software segment grows 2% in headline terms while the company describes it as a growth engine.

🔴 **Insider behaviour.** Zero open-market purchases against five sales (3,792 shares) — no insider has bought this decline.

🟢 **Cash generation is real.** $961M trailing free cash flow, 28% growth, 0.2% capital intensity, 1.23 income quality. The earnings are cash.

🟢 **The platform business is genuinely inflecting.** Platform annual recurring revenue $413M, up 62%, crossing above non-platform for the first time in company history (Q3 FY26); platform net revenue retention 148%; trailing bookings $128M, up 39%. Excluding migrations, platform revenue still grew in the high 30s. This is not an accounting artifact.

🟢 **The predictiveness claim is independently validated.** Milliman, an outside actuarial firm working on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's own released loan-level data, found Score 10T beats VantageScore 4.0 on all three statistical measures, in every origination year, with more than a 10% advantage on first-time buyers. This is the strongest asset the company has, and it is third-party, not self-reported.

🟢 **Guidance delivery.** Six raises or beats in seven quarters, with an openly stated haircut methodology.

🟢 **Score 10T reaches the Federal Housing Administration on 1 January 2027** — a fixed, binding date, announced by the housing department and confirmed by the company on 2026-09-11.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The pricing architecture changed before the narrative did.** Moving the direct-licence programme from $4.95 per score plus a $33 funding fee to $0.99 per score plus a $65 funding fee (April 2026) is the most informative disclosure in six calls. It shifts FICO from being paid per credit pull to being paid per closed loan. That is precisely the design you adopt when you expect to lose control of the pull. Management presented it as pro-competitive goodwill. It is a hedge.

**"Degrees of freedom."** Lansing, July 2026: "we have lots of degrees of freedom in how to respond." In a company that has raised price every single year without hesitation, the refusal to say which direction the next move goes is itself the signal.

**One could easily imagine a revenue jump.** Also July 2026, on whether 10T might be unbundled and charged separately: "One could easily imagine a revenue jump at FICO if we were to charge separately for the two. But that's not the current plan." Management is telling the market there is a price lever left — and simultaneously that the political climate makes pulling it unattractive.

**The Accenture partnership is a distribution admission.** Pairing FICO Platform with Accenture (July 2026) with "phased-in geographic rollout" concedes that direct enterprise selling has not scaled the platform fast enough on its own. The fourth-quarter guidance explicitly carries "incremental front-end loaded marketing expenses" plus "anticipated one-time restructuring charges" to support it.

**The analyst community has gone quiet.** The most recent rating action of any kind is dated 2026-08-12. Nothing has been published since the 4 September collapse. The consensus target of $1,539 and its implied 66% upside are stale by more than six weeks and were all set when the stock traded between $1,038 and $1,373. The one fresh bear — McVeigh at $1,139 on 2026-08-12 — is also stale. Treat the published target set as a historical artifact, not a forward view.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The financial trajectory is strengthening and the strategic trajectory is deteriorating, and the company is actively rebuilding how it gets paid in response. Both statements are true at once, which is why the reported numbers and the share price point in opposite directions.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** *roughly 42% of this company's revenue comes from a price that a federal regulator has publicly attacked, sold through three distributors who each own the competing product, into a channel where the exclusivity requirement was removed on 4 September 2026.* Every valuation that makes FICO look cheap capitalises that revenue at face value. The trailing free cash flow of $961M and the adjusted earnings of $42.43 per share are real — they are also, in substantial part, the proceeds of a price increase from $4.95 to $10 that the company itself will not commit to repeating.

Second, the balance sheet has lost its shock absorber. Management borrowed $1.5B to buy $1.96B of stock at $1,149 in the June quarter, nine weeks before the regulatory decision. Net leverage is 4.2x against peers at 1.4x to 2.4x, 40% of it floating, in a tightening cycle. That converts what would be an earnings problem at an unlevered company into an equity problem here. It is the reason the adverse case is as wide as it is.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is a blend of **intangible brand** (seventy years of model history, the score consumers and lenders name by default) and what was, until three weeks ago, a **regulatory licence** (the government-sponsored enterprises accepted no other score). The returns evidence looks superb and improving — return on invested capital 59% trailing and rising from 41%, gross margin 82.2% and expanding, operating margin up 479 basis points year over year. On the numbers alone this reads as *widening*.

It is not, and the reason is that the numbers measure a mandate that no longer exists. On 4 September 2026 the housing-finance regulator directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to accept VantageScore 4.0 from every originator, effective immediately, and on 9 September the enterprises removed the prior-approval requirement; from 1 January 2027 the Federal Housing Administration accepts all three models. The regulatory-licence half of the moat has been withdrawn by administrative action. What remains is the intangible-brand half plus a genuine, independently-verified predictiveness advantage — a real moat, but a **competitive** one that must be defended on merit and price, not a monopoly one that collects rent. That is **NARROW**, and the trend is **ERODING**, because the price umbrella is being dismantled from two directions at once: by the regulator above and by distributors below who sell the substitute at $0.99 to $4.50 against FICO's $10.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** Lenders will keep pulling FICO scores — the loan-level pricing grids, the securitisation conventions and the model history all embed it, and the predictiveness advantage is documented on the enterprises' own data. What is genuinely at risk is the *price*, not the existence. This does not map onto any of the standard structural-decline forces; it is an idiosyncratic de-monopolisation by regulatory fiat, and it should be tagged as such rather than forced into a theme.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither, and that is the uncomfortable answer. The base is not structurally shrinking, so this is not a value trap. But the cheapness is measured against an earnings base that contains a price increase under active political attack, so it is not a clean fear-print either. It is a peak-earnings question wearing a discount's clothing, and it should be sized as one.

Almost none of that growth is volume. It is the calendar-2026 rate card, which took the mortgage score from $4.95 to $10. In the March 2026 quarter the same line grew 127%. This is a price increase being reported as growth, and it carries close to 100% incremental margin, which is why the margin expansion looks so impressive and why it is so fragile.

That price is now indefensible in the open. On 4 September 2026 the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to accept VantageScore 4.0 from every approved originator, effective immediately, ending a four-month pilot that had been capped at 50 lenders; on 9 September the enterprises removed the prior-written-approval requirement entirely. The agency's director publicly criticised Fair Isaac's pricing, citing roughly an 1,800% increase in the per-score price since 2020, following an investigation opened by Senator Hawley in March. The shares fell about 21% in a single session on 4 September and are 53% below their 52-week high of $1,998.

The distribution structure makes this worse than a normal competitive threat. Fair Isaac does not sell scores to lenders; the three credit bureaus do. Those same bureaus own VantageScore. Equifax is selling VantageScore 4.0 at $4.50, more than 50% below the FICO price, through the end of 2027; TransUnion cut it to $0.99 and is bundling it free with a FICO purchase through 2026. Fair Isaac's distributors are its competitor's owners, and they are now pricing the substitute at a tenth of its price with the regulator's blessing.

Management's defence is that score shopping requires pulling both scores, so FICO keeps the pull. That defence depends on the rival score costing money. It does not. And management admitted on the same July 2026 call that it cannot independently verify the point: asked how easily it could detect volume loss, Lansing answered it is not that easy, honestly, it is not that easy. One quarter earlier, in April 2026, the company had told the market it did not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical. By July the rival was near 20% share at UWM and Rocket. A forward statement of that importance, reversed in 91 days, is a forecasting record the market should not extrapolate from.

The balance sheet has lost its shock absorber. In the June 2026 quarter, nine weeks before the regulatory decision, the company bought back 1.705 million shares for $1.96 billion at an average price of $1,149 and part-funded it with a new $1.5 billion term loan. Across fiscal 2026 it spent roughly $2.7 billion on its own stock at an average near $1,195, against $928.30 today: about $600 million of value destroyed in nine months. Total debt is $5.58 billion at a 5.64% weighted average rate, net debt roughly $5.35 billion, and net leverage 4.2 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, against 1.4 times at S&P Global, 1.5 at Moody's and 2.4 at Verisk. Forty per cent of that debt is floating-rate term loans and revolver, in the month the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time since 2023 with sixteen of eighteen policymakers pointing to another. Leverage turns an earnings problem into an equity problem.

The second business does not yet carry the company. Software grew 2% in the June quarter. The legacy book is shrinking 25% in revenue and 17% in recurring revenue with an 82% retention rate. The platform half is genuinely excellent but is still only $413 million of recurring revenue against a $20 billion market value.

Finally, the mortgage market itself offers no rescue. Lansing said in July 2026 that elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges continue to weigh on the mortgage market, keeping loan originations below historical norms. Since then the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007 and the thirty-year mortgage sits near 6.95%. Any thesis requiring a volume recovery is a rate-cut thesis, and rates are going the other way.

What confirms the bear: a calendar-2027 rate card published at a materially lower price, the first quarter in which FICO pull volume falls below mortgage application volume, or another quarter of the direct-licence certification failing to arrive. On a reduced price and a lost share of pulls, the parts are worth roughly $420 a share.

That logic holds only while the rival score costs real money. It does not. TransUnion cut VantageScore 4.0 to $0.99 and bundles it free with a FICO purchase through 2026; Equifax sells it at $4.50, more than half off, through the end of 2027. When the second pull is free, shopping costs a lender nothing and the substitution shows up at the submission, then at the pull. Management conceded it cannot independently verify this, answering that it is not that easy to detect volume loss.

The second wrong assumption is embedded in our own screener rather than in the street. The headline margin of safety of 109% rests on a single model, a Buffett-style owner-earnings valuation at $1,936. Four of the five methods read negative: discounted cash flow at minus 100%, earnings power value at minus 100%, owner earnings at minus 100%, a fifteen-percent intrinsic value at minus 68%. The one outlier capitalises trailing free cash flow of $961 million, and roughly 42% of the revenue behind it comes from a mortgage score whose price went from $4.95 to $10 in a single year on low-single-digit volume growth. Capitalising that as a perpetuity values the exclusivity at full price three weeks after it ended. This is a peak-earnings artifact, not a discount.

Recurring revenue of $413 million growing 62%, with 148% revenue retention, crossing above the legacy book for the first time in company history, is a real asset that the 2% headline segment growth conceals. moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, at a low conviction, and the reason is narrow enough to state in one sentence: the crash did not create a discount, because the earnings that make the shares look cheap are the very thing the regulator just attacked.

Start with what is not in dispute. Fair Isaac is an exceptional business. It earns a 59% return on invested capital, converts 38 cents of every revenue dollar into free cash flow, spends 0.2% of revenue on capital equipment, scored 8 out of 9 on the Piotroski financial-strength checklist and carries an 8.9 solvency reading. In the June 2026 quarter it grew revenue 26% and reported earnings 41%, expanded its adjusted operating margin 479 basis points to 62%, and raised full-year guidance to $2.53 billion of revenue and $42.43 of adjusted earnings a share. Its Score 10T model was independently confirmed by Milliman, working on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's own released data, to beat the rival on all three measures of predictive power in every origination year. None of that is in doubt.

The problem is where the profit comes from. In the June quarter, mortgage-origination scores were 62% of the Scores segment and Scores was 68% of the company - roughly 42% of total revenue from one product in one channel. That line grew 97% year on year on low-single-digit volume growth, and 127% the quarter before. It is a price increase, from $4.95 to $10 on the calendar-2026 card, being reported as growth, at close to 100% incremental margin. That price existed because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac accepted no other score.

On 4 September 2026 that condition was withdrawn. The Federal Housing Finance Agency directed the enterprises to accept VantageScore 4.0 from every approved originator effective immediately, its director publicly criticised the roughly 1,800% rise in the per-score price since 2020, and on 9 September the approval requirement was removed entirely. The shares fell about 21% in a session. Two of the three bureaus that distribute FICO scores also own the rival and are selling it at $0.99 and $4.50 against FICO's $10. From 1 January 2027 the Federal Housing Administration opens to all three models.

Management's defence is that score shopping forces lenders to pull both scores, so no volume is lost. That is a real argument and it held through June. It depends on the rival costing money, and TransUnion is giving it away free with a FICO purchase. Management also conceded in the same call that it cannot independently verify the point. And one quarter before that call, in April 2026, the company had told the market it did not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical; by July the rival was near 20% share at the two largest originators. That is not a small forecasting miss on a secondary topic - it is the central question, wrong, in 91 days.

So we ran the parts. Scores at $1.4 billion of fiscal 2027 operating profit on 18 times, a quarter below Moody's, for the loss of exclusivity. Software at 3.1 times about $920 million of recurring revenue, blending a platform half compounding above 60% with a legacy half shrinking 25%. Corporate overhead of $335 million a year capitalised at 14 times. Less net debt of about $4.6 billion after a year of paying it down. That gives roughly $880 a share against $928.30 today, or about 25 times fiscal 2027 reported earnings - in line with where the whole data and analytics group trades now. The favourable case, on the 2027 price holding, is about $1,195. The adverse case, on a 30% price cut and a fifth of the pulls lost, is about $420.

That shape is the whole argument. The central outcome is no gain from here, and the adverse case takes away more than half. There is no floor to catch it: tangible asset value is negative at about minus $4.9 billion, there is no deal, no tender, no net cash - only $5.35 billion of net debt ranking ahead of the shareholder.

Two further things tilt it. First, the peer lever that framed this as a bargain does not survive checking. The supplied comparison anchored on data and analytics peers at 35 to 45 times cash flow. As of today they are at 21 to 29 times; Fair Isaac at 25.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow is in line with the median and at a 25% premium on operating earnings, with the worst leverage in the group at 4.2 times against 1.4 to 3.0. The cohort de-rated together on shared drivers - mortgage volume and federal credit-score policy - so that gap is sector movement, not an edge specific to this company. Second, the market regime works against the volume half of the bull case. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September 2026 with most policymakers pointing to another, the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007 and the thirty-year mortgage sits near 6.95%. Any part of the thesis requiring an origination recovery is a rate-cut thesis, and we discount those rather than pay for them.

On the catalyst: the event that mattered has already happened and the fall it caused is spent. In this book that is neither a mark for nor against - we judge the value left over, and the value left over is roughly the price. The same reasoning applies to the fixed 1 January 2027 date at the Federal Housing Administration: it is real and binding, but it admits the rival on the same day, so it is not an asymmetry in this company's favour.

One finding deserves separate weight when sizing. In the June 2026 quarter, nine weeks before the regulatory decision, the company bought 1.705 million shares for $1.96 billion at an average of $1,149 and part-funded it with a new $1.5 billion term loan. Across fiscal 2026 it spent roughly $2.7 billion at an average near $1,195, against $928.30 now - about $600 million of value destroyed in nine months, and the leverage that paid for it is why the adverse case costs the shareholder 55% while the business itself falls 46%. It also means the natural buyer of this dip has told the market it is sidelined while it pays the debt down. A board that levered into the top of its own regulatory cliff has earned a discount on the benefit of the doubt.

What would change this view, specifically: a calendar-2027 rate card published at or near $10, confirming the pricing power survived; or a price in the mid-$600s, which would put the shares roughly 25% below our base reckoning of the parts and start paying us for the regulatory tail. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO)

**Prepared 2026-09-22 · price used $928.30 (NYSE, US dollars) · transcripts covered: Q2 FY25 (2025-04-29) through Q3 FY26 (2026-07-29, pulled live because the archived file stops at 2026-04-28)**

Fair Isaac sells two things. The first is the FICO Score — the credit score that roughly nine in ten large American lenders use, and which until three weeks ago was effectively the only score Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac would accept on a mortgage. The second is FICO Platform, enterprise software that banks use to make lending and fraud decisions. The Score business is small in revenue and enormous in profit; the software business is the reverse. Almost everything that matters about this company right now concerns the first one.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**Spring 2025 — the price lever is working, quietly.** In the April 2025 call management led with 15% revenue growth and mortgage-origination revenue up 48% on a modest price increase. Score 10T, the newer model, was being given away free alongside the classic score to build adoption. The story was: a durable franchise, priced below its worth, gradually closing the gap.

**Summer 2025 — the regulator arrives.** By July 2025 the tone had shifted to defence. Lansing referenced "the recent FHFA announcement" and immediately pivoted to adoption statistics — $313 billion of annualised originations signed to the 10T adopter programme. The subtext: when the mandate goes, adoption will be our moat instead.

**Autumn 2025 — deliberate conservatism.** The November 2025 call is the most revealing on guidance philosophy. Weber: "we build a model that we believe is what's likely to happen. And then we will take that and haircut that expectation… it's probably a little bit more of a haircut that went into that because there's so much uncertainty." Lansing added that although "there's a good chance rates will come down, big volume increases associated with rate declines are not built into our guidance." This is a management team that has systematically under-promised — and, as Section 4 shows, has been rewarded for it.

**Winter–spring 2026 — the price shock lands, and so does the regulator's counter.** The calendar-2026 rate card took the mortgage score from $4.95 to $10. Second-quarter fiscal 2026 (April 2026) was the blow-off: revenue up 39%, Scores up 60%, **mortgage-origination revenue up 127% year over year** on low-single-digit volume growth. Almost all of that was price. In the same call management disclosed it had rewritten the pricing architecture for its direct-licence programme — from $4.95 per score plus a $33 funding fee to **$0.99 per score plus a $65 funding fee** — an explicit move from charging per credit pull to charging per closed loan. That is a defensive redesign dressed as an innovation, and it was announced the week after the housing regulator's credit-score modernisation update.

**Summer 2026 — the story contracts.** By July 2026 the growth rate had halved (Scores up 41%, mortgage revenue up 97%), and Lansing was conceding what he had denied one quarter earlier: VantageScore was running near 20% of conforming volume at the largest originators. His framing — that lenders "game" by pulling both scores, so FICO loses no volume — is the load-bearing assumption of the entire remaining bull case.

**The arc in one line:** a pricing story that compounded for four years has become a regulatory story, and management's narrative has moved from *how much more can we charge* to *how do we keep getting paid at all*.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Growth is broad-based across the franchise | Q2–Q3 FY26 | Scores $459M (+41%) versus Software $215M (**+2%**). Within Scores, mortgage originations are 62% of segment revenue. Mortgage revenue +97% on **low-single-digit** volume | **Diverges sharply.** Company growth is one product line's price increase. Strip mortgage price and the business grows in the high single digits. |
| "We do not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical" | Q2 FY26 (2026-04-28) | One quarter later Lansing: "we have a week of numbers that have a 2 handle on them… we don't anticipate more than the 20s for Vantage share" | **Contradicted by management itself in 91 days.** The most important forward statement of the year, reversed without an acknowledgement that it had been reversed. |

This is pricing, not efficiency. |

Q3: **1,705,000 shares for $1.96B at $1,149**, part-funded by a new $1.5B term loan. Roughly $2.7B spent at an average near $1,195 | **Materially poor.** At $928.30 today that is roughly $600M of value destroyed in nine months, and it was done with borrowed money two months before the regulator removed the company's exclusivity. |

The single most important line in the table is the third. A company that tells the market in April it expects no share loss anywhere, and in July reports a competitor at 20% share in its largest vertical, has either a forecasting problem or a disclosure problem. Neither is priced as a risk today.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — and the decline is in the answers, not the prepared remarks.**

The scripted portions stay uniformly confident across all six calls. The change is in the question-and-answer sessions.

- *April 2025:* expansive and offensive. Kenya scores, financial-literacy campaigns, the mortgage simulator. Growth language throughout.
- *November 2025:* first defensive note, framed as prudence. "It's a lot easier to raise your guidance than it is to lower it."
- *April 2026:* asked whether pilot lenders had received the updated loan-level pricing grid from the regulator, Lansing answered: "No idea. I have heard nothing, I encourage you guys to keep asking the questions, what's going on there?" A chief executive asking sell-side analysts to find out what his regulator is doing is a visibility problem stated out loud.
- *July 2026:* asked how easily the company could even detect volume loss, Lansing: "It's not that easy. It's not — I mean, honestly, it's not that easy. But relative to our forecast and expectations, we're not seeing it." Asked what FICO would do about pricing in response, he declined: "there are many, many things that FICO can do and we're not in a position to share them on this call."

The vocabulary has shifted from *monetisation* and *innovation* to *gaming*, *degrees of freedom*, *theoretical maximum* and *we'll have to wait and see*. Guidance has become **more** specific on the numbers and **less** specific on the drivers — the classic pattern of a management team confident in the next two quarters and unwilling to describe the two after that.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability on delivery: High. Reliability on strategic forecasting: Low.**

The delivery record is close to unimpeachable. Fiscal 2025 guidance was exceeded "on all metrics." Fiscal 2026 guidance was reiterated in the first quarter, raised in the second and raised again in the third, ending at $2.53B of revenue (+20%), $36.86 of reported earnings per share (+39%) and $42.43 on the adjusted basis (+42%). The screener's 6-of-7 quarterly beat rate (86%) matches. Weber describes the sandbagging openly, which is itself a credibility marker — a team that tells you it haircuts its own model is not hiding the haircut.

The strategic forecasting record is the opposite. Three specific failures:

1. **Competitive share.** "We do not anticipate share loss competition in any vertical" (April 2026) survived one quarter.
2. **The direct-licence programme.** Promised as imminent since the first quarter of fiscal 2026 ("one large reseller is close to completing production integration testing"), it is still, in July 2026, "waiting on certification from one of the GSEs so that we can go live." Three consecutive quarters of *almost*. Management's defence — Lansing in January 2026, "whether it comes a little sooner or a little later, does not have a big revenue impact on us" — was then contradicted in July when Weber attributed part of the guidance *raise* to the programme **not** going live, because going live would have pushed revenue out.
3. **Detectability.** The company cannot independently verify its own volume share and says so.

The pattern: FICO is highly reliable about what it will earn in the next ninety days and unreliable about the structure of its market beyond that. For a name whose entire investment case is now structural rather than quarterly, that is the wrong half of the record to be good at.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts have been circling the same three questions for six quarters and have not been given an answer to any of them.

**Where does the price go next year?** Asked by Huber (January 2026) and Clinch (July 2026). Weber: "We don't disclose the specifics of it." Lansing, July 2026: "it's early days… No final decisions have been made about other — about any of the sectors, frankly, about mortgage or auto or card or personal." The calendar-2027 rate card is the single most valuable undisclosed number in the story and management will not be drawn on it.

**Are lenders actually dropping FICO pulls at submission?** Haas (Wells Fargo) and Sabadra (RBC) both asked directly in July 2026. Lansing's answer rests entirely on the gaming argument: you must pull both scores to know which flatters the borrower, therefore FICO's pull volume is protected. This holds only while both scores cost real money. TransUnion is bundling VantageScore 4.0 free with a FICO purchase through 2026, and Equifax is selling it at $4.50 against FICO's $10 through the end of 2027. The moment gaming becomes free, the argument that gaming protects FICO's volume inverts.

Lansing conceded the point: "that's kind of a shopping — a score shopping environment," and that retiring the classic score is "hard to imagine… not anytime soon." A franchise that must live inside a score-shopping market is not the franchise the multiple was built on.

**The question nobody asked:** not one analyst across six calls pressed management on the wisdom of spending $2.7B on its own stock at an average near $1,195, $1.96B of it borrowed, while the company's exclusivity was under active regulatory review. ## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Concentration.** Mortgage-origination scores are 62% of Scores revenue and Scores is 68% of the company — roughly **42% of total revenue from one product in one regulated channel**, at near-100% incremental margin (Q3 FY26).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The pricing architecture changed before the narrative did.** Moving the direct-licence programme from $4.95 per score plus a $33 funding fee to $0.99 per score plus a $65 funding fee (April 2026) is the most informative disclosure in six calls. It shifts FICO from being paid per credit pull to being paid per closed loan. That is precisely the design you adopt when you expect to lose control of the pull. Management presented it as pro-competitive goodwill. It is a hedge.

**"Degrees of freedom."** Lansing, July 2026: "we have lots of degrees of freedom in how to respond." In a company that has raised price every single year without hesitation, the refusal to say which direction the next move goes is itself the signal.

**One could easily imagine a revenue jump.** Also July 2026, on whether 10T might be unbundled and charged separately: "One could easily imagine a revenue jump at FICO if we were to charge separately for the two. But that's not the current plan." Management is telling the market there is a price lever left — and simultaneously that the political climate makes pulling it unattractive.

**The Accenture partnership is a distribution admission.** Pairing FICO Platform with Accenture (July 2026) with "phased-in geographic rollout" concedes that direct enterprise selling has not scaled the platform fast enough on its own. The fourth-quarter guidance explicitly carries "incremental front-end loaded marketing expenses" plus "anticipated one-time restructuring charges" to support it.

**The analyst community has gone quiet.** The most recent rating action of any kind is dated 2026-08-12. Nothing has been published since the 4 September collapse. The consensus target of $1,539 and its implied 66% upside are stale by more than six weeks and were all set when the stock traded between $1,038 and $1,373. The one fresh bear — McVeigh at $1,139 on 2026-08-12 — is also stale. Treat the published target set as a historical artifact, not a forward view.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The financial trajectory is strengthening and the strategic trajectory is deteriorating, and the company is actively rebuilding how it gets paid in response. Both statements are true at once, which is why the reported numbers and the share price point in opposite directions.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** *roughly 42% of this company's revenue comes from a price that a federal regulator has publicly attacked, sold through three distributors who each own the competing product, into a channel where the exclusivity requirement was removed on 4 September 2026.* Every valuation that makes FICO look cheap capitalises that revenue at face value. The trailing free cash flow of $961M and the adjusted earnings of $42.43 per share are real — they are also, in substantial part, the proceeds of a price increase from $4.95 to $10 that the company itself will not commit to repeating.

Second, the balance sheet has lost its shock absorber. Management borrowed $1.5B to buy $1.96B of stock at $1,149 in the June quarter, nine weeks before the regulatory decision. Net leverage is 4.2x against peers at 1.4x to 2.4x, 40% of it floating, in a tightening cycle. That converts what would be an earnings problem at an unlevered company into an equity problem here. It is the reason the adverse case is as wide as it is.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is a blend of **intangible brand** (seventy years of model history, the score consumers and lenders name by default) and what was, until three weeks ago, a **regulatory licence** (the government-sponsored enterprises accepted no other score). The returns evidence looks superb and improving — return on invested capital 59% trailing and rising from 41%, gross margin 82.2% and expanding, operating margin up 479 basis points year over year. On the numbers alone this reads as *widening*.

It is not, and the reason is that the numbers measure a mandate that no longer exists. On 4 September 2026 the housing-finance regulator directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to accept VantageScore 4.0 from every originator, effective immediately, and on 9 September the enterprises removed the prior-approval requirement; from 1 January 2027 the Federal Housing Administration accepts all three models. The regulatory-licence half of the moat has been withdrawn by administrative action. What remains is the intangible-brand half plus a genuine, independently-verified predictiveness advantage — a real moat, but a **competitive** one that must be defended on merit and price, not a monopoly one that collects rent. That is **NARROW**, and the trend is **ERODING**, because the price umbrella is being dismantled from two directions at once: by the regulator above and by distributors below who sell the substitute at $0.99 to $4.50 against FICO's $10.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** Lenders will keep pulling FICO scores — the loan-level pricing grids, the securitisation conventions and the model history all embed it, and the predictiveness advantage is documented on the enterprises' own data. What is genuinely at risk is the *price*, not the existence. This does not map onto any of the standard structural-decline forces; it is an idiosyncratic de-monopolisation by regulatory fiat, and it should be tagged as such rather than forced into a theme.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither, and that is the uncomfortable answer. The base is not structurally shrinking, so this is not a value trap. But the cheapness is measured against an earnings base that contains a price increase under active political attack, so it is not a clean fear-print either. It is a peak-earnings question wearing a discount's clothing, and it should be sized as one.

bull_thesis:

The business outside mortgage pricing is intact and elite. Over the five fiscal years to September 2025 revenue grew from $1.32 billion to $1.99 billion and earnings per share from $13.40 to $26.54, about 18.6% a year. In the June 2026 quarter revenue was $674 million, up 26%, GAAP earnings were $10.45 a share, up 41%, and trailing free cash flow reached roughly $1 billion on capital spending of about 0.2% of revenue. On the 29 July 2026 call management said the 10T adopter programme covers 70 lenders, about 55% of the volume of the top 50 originators, and 10T opens to Federal Housing Administration lenders on 1 January 2027. On 6 October 2026 United Wholesale Mortgage, the largest wholesale lender, reaffirmed FICO on all broker pulls. Card, auto and personal lending - most of the non-mortgage Scores book - face no comparable regulatory change.

Software is a second, under-noticed asset: platform revenue grew 66% in the June quarter while the legacy book shrank 25%, so the segment's flat 2% headline hides a fast-growing recurring business.

Conditions that must hold: the calendar-2027 mortgage price is cut modestly (not halved), lenders keep pulling FICO alongside the rival because score shopping requires both, and free cash flow keeps paying down debt. If so, the parts are worth about $920 a share and the stock re-rates on the November print.

The bear case is that the earnings which make the stock look cheap are the earnings the regulator just took apart, and that the leverage puts the equity first in line for the loss.

In the June 2026 quarter mortgage-origination revenue was about 62% of the $459 million Scores segment and Scores was 68% of the company - roughly 42% of total revenue from one product sold into one regulated channel. That line grew 97% on low-single-digit volume, so the growth was a price increase (the calendar-2026 card took the per-score price from $4.95 to about $10) earned at close to 100% incremental margin.

forcing_function: The event that forces a re-rating is the calendar-2027 mortgage score price, most likely disclosed with or around fiscal Q4 2026 results in early November 2026 (about 25 days away). No activist, asset sale or takeover path is visible; leverage near four times operating earnings rules out a financial buyer.
valley_of_death: There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall - trailing free cash flow is about $1 billion and capital spending is negligible. First, fiscal Q4 2026 results in early November 2026: the first quarter with the rival broadly accepted, carrying about $27 million of severance from the 15% workforce cut, higher interest on the June term loan and, most importantly, the first evidence on pull volume. positioning_washout: There is no dividend and no yield holder base, so forced selling here comes from style mechanics: the stock left momentum, quality-growth and low-volatility screens as it fell 59% from its high.
